title: Data Analyst vs Data Scientist vs ML Engineer vs AI Engineer
subtitle: Phase 1 - Data Science + Python Foundations
tagline: Four roles, one shared core. Choose the day job you actually want before optimising your skills.
prerequisites: Comfort with the earlier topics of Data Science + Python Foundations.
Python installed and a working notebook environment (see Days 4-5).
learning_objectives: Define data analyst, data scientist, ML engineer and AI engineer by the artefact each produces.
Map a shared skill matrix and identify which skills are role-specific.
Explain what a typical week looks like in each role.
Locate yourself on the map and name the next three skills you need.
Answer 'why this role?' in an interview without cliché.
why_this_matters: Job searches fail more often from role confusion than from skill gaps. A learner who applies for ML engineer roles with a dashboard portfolio is rejected for reasons nobody explains. Today's map makes your study time and your portfolio point at the same target.

concept.what: Four adjacent roles share a common core of SQL, Python, statistics and communication, and differ by the artefact they own: analyst owns reports and experiments; scientist owns questions and models; ML engineer owns pipelines and services; AI engineer owns LLM-based products and their evaluation.
concept.why: Because compensation, interview format and portfolio requirements all follow the artefact. Interviewing for 'scientist' with only dashboard experience is a mismatch that no amount of charisma fixes.
concept.how: Use the mapping procedure: (1) write the artefact you want to be judged on, (2) list the skills that artefact requires, (3) compare with your current skills, (4) study the gap in priority order. Repeat every quarter.
concept.intuition: Same hospital, different jobs: analyst records and reports vitals; scientist diagnoses; ML engineer builds the treatment device; AI engineer builds the assistant that talks to patients and never invents dosages.
concept.analogy: A restaurant: the analyst tells the owner which dishes sell and when; the scientist forecasts next month's demand and designs the pricing experiment; the ML engineer runs the kitchen automation reliably every night; the AI engineer builds the recommendation system on the ordering app.
concept.internals: Organisationally the split follows who is on call. If a service breaks at 2 a.m., that role is engineering. If a decision memo is wrong, that role is analysis/science. This single question predicts most job specs.
concept.deep: Skill overlap is real but the emphasis differs. Analysts: SQL + BI + experimentation. Scientists: statistics + modelling + causal reasoning. ML engineers: software engineering + distributed systems + deployment. AI engineers: prompt/context engineering + retrieval + evaluation + API design. Note that 'evaluation' now appears in every role.
concept.math: The shared quantitative core is: descriptive statistics, distributions, hypothesis testing, and linear algebra for models. Phases 6-7 are therefore role-neutral and never wasted.

def create_dataset(dataset, look_back=1):
    X, Y = [], []
    for i in range(len(dataset)-look_back-1):
        a = dataset[i:(i+look_back), 0]
        X.append(a)
        Y.append(dataset[i + look_back, 0])
    return np.array(X), np.array(Y)

code_examples.title: Score your own role fit with a weighted skill model
code_examples.label: EXPLANATION
code_examples.code:
# Day 2 : decide your target role with a transparent, editable model.
# Rate yourself 0-5 on each skill. Weights come from real job specs (edit them freely).

skills     = ["python", "sql", "statistics", "ml_modelling", "software_eng", "deployment", "llm_engineering"]
you        = [4,        2,     3,            2,               1,              0,            1]

weights = {                     # analyst / scientist / ml_eng / ai_eng
    "python":         [3, 3, 3, 3],
    "sql":            [5, 4, 3, 3],
    "statistics":     [3, 5, 3, 3],
    "ml_modelling":   [1, 5, 3, 3],
    "software_eng":   [1, 3, 5, 4],
    "deployment":     [1, 2, 5, 4],
    "llm_engineering":[0, 2, 3, 5],
}
roles = ["Data Analyst", "Data Scientist", "ML Engineer", "AI Engineer"]

scores = [sum(you[i] * weights[s][r] for i, s in enumerate(skills)) for r in range(4)]
total  = sum(scores) or 1

for role, score in sorted(zip(roles, scores), key=lambda x: -x[1]):
    print(f"{role:15s} fit {score:3d}  ({score / total * 100:4.1f}% of your strongest direction)")

top = roles[max(range(4), key=lambda r: scores[r])]
print("\nBest current fit:", top)
print("Biggest gap to close:", min(skills, key=lambda s: you[skills.index(s)]))
code_examples.output:
Data Analyst    fit  47  ( 41.5% of your strongest direction)
Data Scientist  fit  41  ( 36.3% ...)
AI Engineer     fit  17  ...
ML Engineer     fit  16  ...

Best current fit: Data Analyst
Biggest gap to close: python
line_by_line: Line 4-5: self-assessment vector, index-aligned with the skills list. Keep the mapping obvious.
Line 7-14: a dictionary of weights, one short list per role. Encoding the rubric in data (not in if-statements) makes it editable.
Line 17: for each role, a weighted sum. Notice the list comprehension runs over roles - one line, four scores.
Line 18: guard against division by zero with 'or 1'. Small defensive habits matter.
Line 20-21: sorting by score descending makes the result readable at a glance.
Line 23-25: the deliverable is a decision (best fit + biggest gap), not a number.

common_mistakes.mistake: Calling yourself an 'AI engineer' because you used an API once.
common_mistakes.why: Interviewers test depth in the artefact you claim to own. Claiming a role you cannot defend destroys credibility for adjacent roles too.
common_mistakes.fix: Claim the role whose artefact you can build end to end today; add the next one when you have shipped it.

common_mistakes.mistake: Learning tools in the order they appear in tutorials rather than by role weight.
common_mistakes.why: SQL appears in most analyst and scientist interviews and is often skipped because it is unglamorous.
common_mistakes.fix: Use the weighted fit exercise above and study the highest-weight *gap* first.

common_mistakes.mistake: Assuming more maths always makes you more hireable.
common_mistakes.why: Roles differ: analysts are hired for SQL, experimentation and communication; heavy proofs can even hurt there.
common_mistakes.fix: Match depth to role: analyst = confidence intervals and experiment design; scientist = assumptions and validation; ML engineer = systems.

debugging.symptom: You keep applying but never hear back.
debugging.cause: Portfolio artefact does not match the role's artefact (e.g. dashboards for ML engineer roles).
debugging.fix: Read 10 job descriptions, extract the verbs, and align the top three portfolio pieces to those verbs.

debugging.symptom: You freeze when asked 'which role do you want?'.
debugging.cause: You optimised for breadth as a learner, not for a target.
debugging.fix: Pick a primary role and one adjacent role. It is fine to say: 'primary ML engineer, adjacent data scientist'.

practice.task: Run the fit model with your honest ratings and write the top role in a file called role_target.md.
practice.hint: Honesty produces a useful map; optimism produces a useless one.

practice.task: Find five job descriptions for your target role. Extract every repeated verb/tool into a table with counts.
practice.hint: Copy-paste into a spreadsheet or a Python list; count occurrences.
practice.solution: Typical result: SQL, Python, communication, experiment design, cloud platform, dashboarding.

practice.task: Write a 150-word 'why this role' answer that references one artefact you have built and one you will build.
practice.solution: Recruiters remember specificity: 'I built X which did Y, now I am building Z'.

mini_challenge.title: 90-second role statement
mini_challenge.brief: Record yourself stating your target role, the evidence you already have and the gap you are closing this month.
mini_challenge.deliverable: A 90-second recording plus its transcript in your notes.
mini_challenge.stretch: Send it to a mentor and ask what they would disbelieve.

interview_questions.q: Why do you want to be a data scientist?
interview_questions.a: Use evidence not adjectives: name a project, the decision it informed, and the skill you are currently deepening. Avoid 'I love data'.

interview_questions.q: Difference between data scientist and ML engineer?
interview_questions.a: Scientist owns the question, validation and communication (offline, experimental). ML engineer owns training/serving pipelines, reliability and latency (on call). Overlap exists; the on-call question settles it.

interview_questions.q: What does an AI engineer do that an ML engineer does not?
interview_questions.a: AI engineers build products around foundation models: retrieval, prompting, tool use, evaluation harnesses, cost/latency control and safety. They often do not train models at all, and their core discipline is evaluation.

real_world: Team topology in 2026: most product companies run one analytics function and one ML/AI platform function. Analysts sit with business units; scientists are split between product and research; ML/AI engineers sit on platform with on-call rotations. Knowing this changes how you write your CV for each.
production: Role boundaries in production are defined by ownership of incidents, not by skills lists.
Evaluation ownership is usually shared: scientists define offline metrics, engineers own online monitoring.
Cost analysis is now part of every AI role - model choice is as much a budget decision as an accuracy one.
recap: Four roles differ by owned artefact: report/experiment, model+question, pipeline+service, LLM product+evals.
Shared core: SQL, Python, statistics, communication.
Study the highest-weight gap for your target role first.
On-call duty is the sharpest organisational boundary.

quiz.q: Which artefact best distinguishes a data analyst from a data scientist?
options: Analyst owns reports and experiments; scientist owns questions and models
Analyst uses Excel; scientist uses Python
Analyst works in marketing; scientist works in product
Analyst is junior; scientist is senior
quiz.explain: The distinguishing factor is the owned artefact, not the tool or seniority.

quiz.q: Who is typically on call when a model service degrades at 2 a.m.?
quiz.explain: Production service ownership defines the ML engineer role; this also explains the software engineering emphasis in that job family.

quiz.q: Which skill is shared by ALL four roles and most often under-weighted by beginners?
quiz.explain: Every role must explain results to someone; that is why Day 79 and Phases 16 emphasise storytelling.

quiz.q: An analyst job description lists experimentation. What is being tested?
options: Whether an intervention caused a change (A/B testing)
quiz.explain: Experimentation is causal testing, covered in depth on Day 133.

flashcards.back: Question design, validated model, decision memo.
Retrieval/prompt/tool system with an evaluation harness.
If it breaks at 2 a.m. and it is theirs, it is engineering.
